16 IKEA gifts for a child: how often can a driver cross into Belarus without customs trouble?

A fictional chauffeur buys ANTILOP, LILLABO, DUKTIG and MÅLA for his child. Understand Belarus’s €500/25 kg allowance, weekly crossings, receipts, duties and EU sanctions.

ComfortLine·Reviewed 3 November 2026
Important: personal information only, not an official legal source

This article is for personal information and trip preparation only. ComfortLine is not a customs or government authority. It is not official law, individual legal advice or a guarantee of clearance. Check current EAEU rules, Belarusian customs guidance, EU export restrictions and the rules of your departure country immediately before travelling. Seek an official written response for uncertain items or circumstances.

500 €Personal-use value ceiling
25 kgPersonal-use weight ceiling
16 IKEAProducts on the shopping list

Meet the driver who had a very small customer

Imagine a ComfortLine chauffeur named Max. His regular route takes him between Belarus and the EU, but the most demanding client is at home: his little child. Max wants to buy an ANTILOP high chair, LOCKIG potty, LILLABO wooden railway, DUKTIG pretend checkout, UNDERHÅLLA abacus and enough MÅLA art supplies for a miniature studio.

Sixteen IKEA article numbers later, the list looks innocent. Yet customs must evaluate what the items cost, what they weigh, how often the driver enters Belarus, whether they are genuinely for his family, and whether EU export sanctions affect their classifications. This is a fictional story illustrating real rules.

The IKEA shopping basket: 16 products for one child

This is the character's wish list, not confirmation that every SKU is currently sold. Names and codes reproduce the supplied list. Verify prices, availability, packages, weights, origins and restrictions in the country of purchase. ANTILOP's three components make up one functional high chair.

The general Belarus/EAEU allowance: €500 AND 25 kg

For ordinary personal-use goods carried into Belarus by road, the EAEU duty-free thresholds are €500 in total value AND 25 kg in total weight per person. Both must be satisfied. A €480 basket weighing 26 kg exceeds the weight test; a €540 basket at 20 kg exceeds the value test. This is an allowance for recognised personal baggage, not an automatic permit to bring commercial orders on a chauffeur trip. [1] [6]

Use genuine receipts, invoices, tags and online-order records to establish value. Without reliable evidence, customs can determine value using available data. Check the real packaged weights rather than relying on an item's dimensions in a product photograph. [7]

Twice a day, every few days, weekly or twice a year

Once every six months: one of each genuinely family-oriented product is easier to explain, subject to the €500/25 kg rules. Weekly: the monetary duty-free threshold does not automatically shrink, but customs considers purpose and frequency. Published Belarusian Customs risk guidance gives a benchmark of up to ten of each item type for travellers crossing no more than once every seven days, always subject to normal household needs—not a promise that ten identical high chairs qualify. [1] [5]

More often than every seven days: guidance narrows the benchmark to one unit of each item type; more often than every three days: it describes only one unit of one item type; more than once in a calendar day: used articles needed for the journey or at the destination. A new 16-item collection on the third crossing in a week deserves particular scrutiny. These are administrative indicators of personal use, not separate tax-free limits or automatic approvals. [5]

The outdated €300/20 kg rule

Old webpages still claim repeat travellers have a €300/20 kg allowance after more than one entry in three months. That came from outdated versions of Belarus's Decree No. 360. Decree No. 146 of April 2020 removed its special threshold, while Decree No. 73 of February 2022 rewrote the previously cited classification paragraph. Presenting the old figures as current law would be misleading. [3] [4]

The general €500/25 kg EAEU limit therefore applies to personal baggage. But repeated deliveries to other people can still be treated as commercial goods even when a particular basket stays under those figures. [1] [5]

If the basket goes over the allowance

For goods still accepted as personal-use items, the standard excess charge is 30% of value above €500, but no less than €4 for each kilogram above 25 kg, under the applicable EAEU calculation. Illustrations: €540 at 24 kg gives €12 for value excess; €400 at 28 kg gives €12 for weight; €600 at 28 kg gives €30, the higher of the €30 value and €12 weight calculations. Additional fees or other rules may apply. [2]

Declare dutiable goods using the red channel. If customs determines the goods are actually commercial, the simple personal-use duty formula may not apply; business customs clearance, taxes and documents could be required. [2] [7]

A gift for your child, or a paid delivery business?

One high-chair set, one potty, some toys and art supplies for Max's own child point toward family use. Weekly paid shopping requests for customers, stacks of matching boxes or repeated orders suggest something different. The words 'for children' on packaging do not transform a commercial consignment into personal baggage. Customs also assesses the full pattern of past crossings. [5] [12]

The three ANTILOP article numbers are sold as components but form a single high chair. Their genuine prices and weights count; family purpose cannot be established by splitting a receipt into separate tickets or assigning purchases artificially to passengers.

EU export restrictions are a separate checkpoint

Belarus's €500 is NOT permission from the EU to export all 16 IKEA products. Lithuania, Latvia and Poland apply EU Regulation 765/2006 and its current annexes. Eligibility depends on the precise CN classification, item descriptions, value, intended use and exceptions. Check potentially affected categories with the departure customs authority before buying. [8] [9] [11]

The often-mentioned €60 issue concerns euro-denominated banknotes, not a universal €60 shopping limit. And the €300 passenger import allowance on entry into Lithuania from Belarus belongs to the opposite direction: it does not cap IKEA purchases being brought into Belarus. [8] [10]

Max's sensible ending

Before driving home, Max saves the 16 IKEA codes, real invoices, package weights and evidence that the items are for his household. He checks whether customs classifications or sanctions need a written answer. Under the right conditions, a personal basket no more than €500 and 25 kg may qualify for duty-free entry—but only after the legal and factual tests are met.

Max's little customer cares about one thing: the LILLABO railway. Max cares about delivering it home instead of spending the evening explaining a suitcase of goods at the border.

Six checks before leaving

  • Check all 16 product codes against the current IKEA catalog and receipts.
  • Total actual purchase values and weights, including relevant packaging.
  • Review how often you entered and whether everything truly serves your family.
  • Check EU export sanctions and item classifications before departure.
  • Prepare declarations and contact customs if thresholds or circumstances are unclear.
  • Check current checkpoints and both countries' requirements immediately before travel.
